profile.feeling: The speaker; the first word of every self-introduction.

senses.def: I (first person singular, masculine and feminine)
the ego, the self (as a noun: הָאֲנִי)

synonyms.nuance: the older Biblical “I”, used today only in elevated or archaic style (it opens the Ten Commandments: אָנֹכִי ה׳)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku, from Proto-Afroasiatic *ʔanāku.

funFacts: The Biblical form אָנֹכִי keeps the k of Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku, like Akkadian anāku; Arabic أَنَا (ʔanā) lost it, as did אֲנִי.
pitfalls: The present-tense verb after אֲנִי shows the speaker’s gender: a man says אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, a woman אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
subtleties: In the past and future the verb ending already means “I” (אָכַלְתִּי “I ate”), so אֲנִי is often dropped; in the present (a participle without person endings) it cannot be dropped.
As a noun, הָאֲנִי means “the ego, the self”.

profile.feeling: Direct address to one man or boy.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Hebrew has no formal “you” (no T/V distinction like German du/Sie) — the same pronoun is used to a friend, a child, a boss or a minister; politeness comes from words like בְּבַקָּשָׁה, not from the pronoun.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanta. Cognate with Arabic أَنْتَ (ʔanta).

funFacts: The dagesh in the ת is the trace of a lost n: Proto-Semitic *ʔanta became *ʔatta — compare Arabic أَنْتَ (ʔanta), which kept the n.
pitfalls: Masculine only: to a woman say אַתְּ. The verb agrees too: אַתָּה רוֹצֶה, but אַתְּ רוֹצָה.
Spelled with a final ה although it is pronounced atá.
subtleties: Hebrew has no polite “you”: אַתָּה is used to everyone, including strangers and superiors.

profile.feeling: Direct address to one woman or girl.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Hebrew has no formal “you” (no T/V distinction like German du/Sie) — the same pronoun is used to a friend, a child, a boss or a minister; politeness comes from words like בְּבַקָּשָׁה, not from the pronoun.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanti.

funFacts: Arabic keeps the vowel that Hebrew lost: أَنْتِ (ʔanti) ~ אַתְּ (at).
pitfalls: Without vowel marks אַתְּ is written את — exactly like the object marker אֶת. Only the context tells them apart.
The verb agrees: אַתְּ רוֹצָה (not אַתְּ רוֹצֶה).
subtleties: The final ת carries a dagesh and a shva — one of the few Hebrew words ending in a consonant cluster (at < *ant).

profile.feeling: A man — or any masculine thing (Hebrew has no “it”).

senses.def: is (present-tense copula linking subject and predicate)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *šuʔa.

funFacts: Arabic هُوَ (huwa) is the same pronoun.
In the Torah scroll the letters הוא are also written for “she”; the vowels turn them into הִוא (read hi).
pitfalls: Hebrew has no neuter: a masculine thing is הוּא too — הַגֶּזֶר? הוּא פֹּה.
subtleties: In the present, הוּא can link subject and predicate like “is”: דָּוִד הוּא מוֹרֶה. It agrees with the subject: הִיא for a feminine subject, הֵם / הֵן for plurals.

profile.feeling: A woman — or any feminine thing.

senses.def: is (present-tense copula for a feminine subject)

examples.tr: She buys lettuce at the market.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *šiʔa.

funFacts: Arabic هِيَ (hiya) is the same pronoun.
In the Torah the word is usually written הוא and pointed הִוא — the scribes’ spelling for “she” in the Five Books.
pitfalls: Feminine nouns are “she”: הָעַגְבָנִיָּה? הִיא פֹּה (The tomato? It’s here.).
Do not confuse הִיא (hi, she) with הוּא (hu, he) — the letters differ only in י / ו.
subtleties: The verb after הִיא takes the feminine form: הִיא אוֹכֶלֶת, הִיא שׁוֹתָה, הִיא רוֹצָה.

profile.feeling: The group, the family, “us”.

senses.def: we (first person plural, masculine and feminine)

synonyms.nuance: the short form of formal writing and speeches (אָנוּ מוֹדִים … “we thank …”)
a rare Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *niḥnu. Cognate with Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu).

funFacts: Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu) is the same word without the initial a-; Hebrew נַחְנוּ also exists (rarely) in the Bible.
pitfalls: אֲנַחְנוּ has no gender; the verb shows it: אֲנַחְנוּ אוֹכְלִים (men or a mixed group), אֲנַחְנוּ אוֹכְלוֹת (women only).
subtleties: The stress is on the middle syllable: a-NACH-nu.

profile.feeling: A group of men, or a mixed group.

senses.def: they (masculine plural, also for mixed groups)
those (distant demonstrative, after a definite noun: הַיָּמִים הָהֵם)

examples.tr: In those days there was no electricity.

synonyms.nuance: a longer Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šum. Cognate with Arabic هُم (hum).

funFacts: Arabic هُم (hum) is the same pronoun.
pitfalls: הֵם is used for any mixed group: nine women and one man are הֵם.
subtleties: With the article, הָהֵם means “those”: הַיָּמִים הָהֵם (those days), as opposed to הַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה (these days).

profile.feeling: A group of women only, or feminine things.

synonyms.nuance: a longer Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šin. Cognate with Arabic هُنَّ (hunna).

funFacts: Arabic هُنَّ (hunna) has the same feminine -n as Hebrew הֵן.
pitfalls: Only for an all-female group or feminine nouns; add one man and it becomes הֵם.
In casual speech many Israelis say הֵם even for women; written and careful Hebrew keeps הֵן.
subtleties: A homograph: the particle הֵן “behold; (formal) yes”.

lexemes.note: No present tense: in the present Hebrew uses a nominal sentence without a verb (הַגֶּזֶר פֹּה “the carrot is here”). The participle הוֹוֶה exists only as a rare literary form, so only past, future and infinitive are stored.

override.V;PST;3;SG;FEM: Wiktionary lists the full and the vocalized spelling as one string “הייתה \ הָיְתָה”; we store the vocalized form הָיְתָה and the full spelling הייתה in plene.

profile.feeling: The invisible verb: everywhere in the past and future, absent in the present.

senses.def: to be (in the past and future; no present form in use)
with לְ: to have (in the past and future: הָיָה לִי “I had”)

collocations.tr: to be or not to be

phrases.meaning: once upon a time — the opening of fairy tales

phrases.tr: what has been is what will be

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: הָיָה is the only verb “to be”; in the present Hebrew uses no verb, or a pronoun as copula (הוּא, הִיא, הֵם, הֵן).

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *haway- (“to fall, happen, be, become”).

funFacts: God’s name in Exodus 3:14 is explained with this verb: אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה “I will be what I will be”.
pitfalls: No present: “the salad is tasty” is הַסָּלָט טָעִים, with no verb at all.
Past and future agree with the subject: הַסָּלָט הָיָה, הָעַגְבָנִיָּה הָיְתָה, הַיְּרָקוֹת הָיוּ; הוּא יִהְיֶה, הִיא תִּהְיֶה.
In possession the verb agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: הָיְתָה לִי עַגְבָנִיָּה (עַגְבָנִיָּה is feminine).
subtleties: הָיָה + a present participle gives a habitual past: הוּא הָיָה אוֹכֵל … “he used to eat …”.
The everyday full spelling of הָיְתָה is הייתה.

profile.feeling: Everyday; in figurative use, being consumed by something.

senses.def: to consume, eat up (figuratively: worry, jealousy)

examples.tr: What do you eat for breakfast?
She eats a lot of vegetables.

phrases.meaning: he was eaten up by regret or worry
I got into trouble, I paid for it

synonyms.nuance: to dine — elevated, literary
to gobble, eat greedily (mocking)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal-. Compare Aramaic אֲכַל (ʾăḵal), Arabic أَكَلَ (ʔakala).

funFacts: אֹכֶל (okhel, food) and מַאֲכָל (ma’akhal, dish) come from the same root א־כ־ל.
pitfalls: The present tense agrees in gender: a man says אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, a woman אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
Future יֹאכַל: the א is silent (yokhal).
subtleties: Slang אָכַלְתִּי אוֹתָהּ has nothing to do with food: ‘I got burned’.

profile.feeling: Water in the heat, coffee in the morning; on its own, often alcohol.

examples.tr: What do you (f.) drink in the morning?

synonyms.nuance: to sip, take a gulp
to gulp down, drink in one go

etymology.text: Compare Aramaic אִשְׁתִּי (ʾištī), Ge’ez ሰትየ (sätyä).

funFacts: מִשְׁתֶּה (a feast, literally “a drinking”), the word for the banquets of the Purim story, comes from the same root.
pitfalls: A lamed-he verb: the present ends in a vowel — שׁוֹתֶה (m), שׁוֹתָה (f); the feminine has no -ֶת ending like אוֹכֶלֶת.
Infinitive לִשְׁתּוֹת (lishtot), with a dagesh in the ת.
subtleties: Without an object, הוּא שׁוֹתֶה can mean “he drinks (alcohol)” — as in English.

profile.feeling: The market, the supermarket, the shopping list.

senses.def: to acquire, to obtain (formal; wisdom, a friend)
to accept as true, to “buy” (a story)

examples.tr: I (m.) buy bread at the grocery shop.
She buys fruit at the market.

examples.text: אֲנִי לֹא קוֹנֶה אֶת הַסִּפּוּר הַזֶּה.

phrases.meaning: make the effort to find a true friend
he won him over, captivated him

synonyms.nuance: to acquire, purchase — written, commercial and official language

etymology.text: Cognate with Aramaic קְנָא (“to acquire”).

funFacts: The present participle is also a noun: קוֹנֶה “buyer, customer”.
Same letters, a different word: קָנֶה “reed, cane” — related to Greek κάννα and to English cane, canal, cannon.
pitfalls: A lamed-he verb like שָׁתָה: קוֹנֶה (m), קוֹנָה (f), קוֹנִים, קוֹנוֹת.
Do not confuse קוֹנָה “(she) buys” with קָנְתָה “she bought”.
subtleties: In the Bible and in formal Hebrew קָנָה means “acquire” in general, not only with money: קְנֵה לְךָ חָבֵר.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses אָהַב only as “to love”; in Modern Hebrew the same verb is the normal way to say “like” for food and activities (אֲנִי אוֹהֵב חֲצִילִים), and the profile shows both senses.

profile.feeling: From “I like salad” to “I love you” — one verb for both.

examples.tr: I love you (a man to a woman).

phrases.tr: and you shall love your neighbour as yourself

synonyms.nuance: to be fond of, to like (people or things) — milder than אָהַב
“dying on” — to be crazy about: אֲנִי מֵת עַל חֲצִילִים
“found favour in my eyes” = I like it; the thing liked is the subject: הַסָּלָט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic 𐎀𐎅𐎁 (ảhb).

funFacts: Hebrew uses one verb for “like” and “love”: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב חֲצִילִים and אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אוֹתָךְ.
אַהֲבָה (love) and אָהוּב (beloved) come from the same root.
pitfalls: A definite object needs אֶת: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הַסָּלָט — but אֲנִי אוֹהֵב סָלָט.
Plural with hataf patah: אוֹהֲבִים, אוֹהֲבוֹת.
subtleties: For people אוֹהֵב is strong (“love”); to say you simply like someone, Hebrew prefers מְחַבֵּב.

profile.feeling: Wishes, orders at the counter, children asking for ice cream.

senses.def: to accept, to be pleased with (Biblical)

examples.tr: What do you (f.) want to eat?

phrases.tr: if you will it, it is no legend
phrases.meaning: determination can make a dream real

synonyms.nuance: “it comes to me” = I feel like (it): בָּא לִי גְּלִידָה; the thing wanted is the subject
to desire, to wish — elevated style

etymology.text: Compare Arabic رَضِيَ (raḍiya).

funFacts: In the Bible רָצָה means “to be pleased with, to accept” — close to its Arabic relative رَضِيَ (raḍiya, “to be satisfied”); “to want” is the later meaning.
pitfalls: Homograph: רָצָה is also “(she) runs” (the present of רָץ). הוּא רָצָה (ratsá) = he wanted; הִיא רָצָה (rátsa) = she runs.
A lamed-he verb: רוֹצֶה (m), רוֹצָה (f).
subtleties: In shops Israelis often ask with אֶפְשָׁר …? (“is it possible …?”) — politer than אֲנִי רוֹצֶה.

lexemes.note: An existential particle (Wiktionary files it as an adverb). Possession: יֵשׁ + לְ + possessor (יֵשׁ לִי); its negation is אֵין.

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s second sense is “someone/something has” (with לְ) — exactly this concept; the check only misses it because the gloss is worded with “has”.

profile.feeling: Hebrew “has” nothing — things “are there for” you: יֵשׁ לִי.

senses.def: with לְ: to have (possession) — יֵשׁ לִי “I have”

examples.tr: Is there milk in the fridge?

phrases.meaning: maybe; it’s possible; is there a chance?

synonyms.nuance: inflected form “he/it is there, exists” (יֶשְׁנוֹ, יֶשְׁנָהּ …), used in formal writing

antonyms.note: there isn’t; (with לְ) not to have

etymology.text: Related to Aramaic אִית (ʾīṯ). Compare Arabic لَيْسَ (laysa, “to not be, there is not”).

funFacts: Wiktionary compares Arabic لَيْسَ (laysa, “is not”), which is often explained as “not” + this same existential word.
pitfalls: יֵשׁ never changes for person: יֵשׁ לִי, יֵשׁ לוֹ, יֵשׁ לָנוּ — the owner is shown by לְ with a suffix.
The negative is אֵין, never *לֹא יֵשׁ: אֵין לִי גֶּזֶר.
Only present: “I had” = הָיָה לִי / הָיְתָה לִי, “I will have” = יִהְיֶה לִי.
subtleties: The thing possessed is grammatically the subject, so standard Hebrew puts no אֶת before it (יֵשׁ לִי הַסֵּפֶר); colloquially יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר is very common.

lexemes.note: The present-tense negation of existence and possession (the opposite of יֵשׁ). Formal Hebrew also inflects it as a negative copula: אֵינֶנִּי / אֵינִי, אֵינְךָ, אֵינוֹ, אֵינָהּ …

profile.feeling: Absence: no milk, no time, no problem.

senses.def: there is not, there are no; with לְ: not to have — the negation of יֵשׁ
is not (formal negative copula, often with a suffix: אֵינוֹ, אֵינָהּ)

examples.tr: There is no milk in the fridge.

phrases.tr: there is nothing new under the sun

phrases.meaning: never mind; it’s nothing (a reply to thanks or an apology)

synonyms.nuance: the general “not” for verbs, adjectives and the past/future; אֵין is only for “there isn’t / don’t have” in the present (and formal negative copula)

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic 𐎛𐎐 (ỉn) and Arabic إِنْ (ʔin).

funFacts: The mystical name אֵין סוֹף (Ein Sof, “the Infinite”) is literally “there is no end”.
Same letters, a different word: אַיִן “nothing, nothingness” (as in יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן).
pitfalls: Never *לֹא יֵשׁ — say אֵין: אֵין לִי גֶּזֶר.
Present only: “there wasn’t” = לֹא הָיָה, “there won’t be” = לֹא יִהְיֶה.
subtleties: Formal style negates a present verb with אֵין + suffix: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ “I do not know”; everyday speech says אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ.

profile.feeling: Agreement, a quick nod.

senses.def: so, thus (in fixed phrases: אַחֲרֵי כֵּן, לָכֵן)

examples.tr: Are you (f.) at home? Yes, I’m at home.

phrases.meaning: may there be many more like it (a congratulation)

synonyms.nuance: “sure!” — an eager, informal yes
“definitely” — an emphatic yes
a formal “yes”, e.g. when voting

etymology.text: Wiktionary records two senses: “yes” and the older “thus, so” (archaic). The old meaning survives in אַחֲרֵי כֵּן (“after so” = afterwards) and לָכֵן (“for so” = therefore); “yes” is the answer “(it is) so”.

funFacts: כֵּן יִרְבּוּ (“may they multiply so”) is a congratulation: “may there be many more like it”.
pitfalls: כֵּן (ken, yes) and כָּאן (kan, here) are easy to confuse: watch the vowel.
subtleties: Israelis often answer a yes/no question by repeating the verb: — אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? — רוֹצֶה.
A homograph is the adjective כֵּן “sincere, honest”.

profile.feeling: The basic “not” — short and firm.

senses.def: not (negates verbs, adjectives, adverbs and whole predicates)

synonyms.nuance: the “not” of prohibitions, with the future: אַל תִּקְנֶה! “don’t buy!”
a poetic “not” in fixed phrases

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *lā. Cognate with Arabic لا.

funFacts: Arabic لا (lā) is the same word: both “not” and “no”.
pitfalls: לֹא stands right before what it negates: הוּא לֹא אוֹכֵל (not after the verb).
For “there isn’t / I don’t have” use אֵין, not לֹא: אֵין לִי זְמַן.
subtleties: Negative words still need לֹא: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם “I want nothing” (literally “I don’t want nothing”).
לֹא + future is an absolute prohibition, as in the Ten Commandments: לֹא תִּרְצָח.

lexemes.note: Same written form and sound as the negation לֹא “not” (he:lo); as an answer it stands alone, usually followed by a pause or comma.

profile.feeling: A clear refusal; Israeli directness.

examples.tr: Do you (f.) want more? No, that’s enough.

synonyms.nuance: “what suddenly?!” — a strong “no way!”
an Aramaic-flavoured “no / not”, alive in fixed phrases: לָאו דַּוְקָא “not necessarily”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *lā. Cognate with Arabic لا.

funFacts: Arabic لا also means both “no” and “not”.
pitfalls: Hebrew uses one word for “no” and “not”: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה (No, I don’t want).
subtleties: Israeli speech is direct: a plain לֹא is not rude, though לֹא, תּוֹדָה is the polite default.

lexemes.note: Written attached to the next word. Normative form וּ (u-) before ב, מ, פ and before a consonant with shva; before a hataf vowel it takes the matching short vowel (וַ before ־ֲ); before יְ it becomes וִי. In the sentence bank only וְ is used.

profile.feeling: The glue of every list.

examples.tr: Dad and Mum are at home.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: וְ is the only “and”; גַּם means “also, too”.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *wa. Cognate with Arabic وَ (wa).

funFacts: Arabic وَ (wa) is written attached in the same way.
pitfalls: Before ב, מ, פ and before a shva the normative form is וּ: גֶּזֶר וּמְלָפְפוֹן; a following ב / כ / פ then loses its dagesh (לֶחֶם וּבָצָל).
Before a hataf vowel it copies the vowel: וַחֲצִילִים; before יְ it becomes וִי: וִירָקוֹת.
It is never written as a separate word.
subtleties: In everyday speech most people say ve- everywhere; u- is heard in careful speech, the news and reading aloud.
In pairs it is sometimes וָ: תֹּהוּ וָבֹהוּ, יוֹם וָלַיְלָה.

profile.feeling: Pointing at things: “this one!”

senses.def: this, this one (demonstrative): זֶה (m), זֹאת (f), אֵלֶּה (pl)

synonyms.nuance: a shorter feminine variant of זֹאת, common in writing
a variant of the plural אֵלֶּה

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ḏV- (“this”). Cognates include Aramaic דִּי (dī) and Arabic ذا. Compare also the definite form הַזֶּה (hazé) and Arabic هٰذَا (hāḏā).

funFacts: Hebrew ז regularly matches Arabic ذ (dh): זֶה ~ ذَا, זָהָב ~ ذَهَب (gold).
pitfalls: Agreement: זֶה for a masculine noun, זֹאת for a feminine one, אֵלֶּה for plurals — זֶה גֶּזֶר, זֹאת עַגְבָנִיָּה, אֵלֶּה גְּזָרִים.
“This is a carrot” is זֶה גֶּזֶר; “this carrot” is הַגֶּזֶר הַזֶּה — after a noun the demonstrative takes the article.
subtleties: In casual speech זֶה is used for everything, even feminine and plural things: זֶה עַגְבָנִיָּה, זֶה טָעִים.

profile.feeling: Curiosity; also surprise and admiration.

phrases.meaning: the Four Questions of the Seder

synonyms.nuance: the classical spelling with patah, followed by a doubled consonant: מַה נִּשְׁתַּנָּה

etymology.text: Cognates such as Aramaic מָה (mā, “what”), Arabic مَا (mā, “what”) and Ugaritic 𐎎𐎅 (mh) can be found across the Central Semitic languages.

funFacts: The Passover Seder’s Four Questions open with מַה נִּשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה — “What makes this night different?”
pitfalls: No verb “is” is needed: מָה זֶה? = What is this?
“Which …?” is usually אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ, not מָה: אֵיזֶה יָרָק? (which vegetable?).
subtleties: מָה alone (“What?!”) can express surprise or impatience, depending on the tone.

profile.feeling: Looking for things, people and places.

senses.def: where (in indirect questions: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אֵיפֹה …)

examples.tr: I (m.) don’t know where he is.

synonyms.nuance: the formal and literary “where”
a poetic, Biblical “where (is)?”

etymology.text: From אֵי (e, “where”) + פֹּה (po, “here”).

funFacts: It is literally “where-here”: אֵי + פֹּה.
Do not confuse it with אֵיפָה “ephah” (a Biblical dry measure): אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה (“an ephah and an ephah”) means a double standard.
pitfalls: “Where to?” is לְאָן, not אֵיפֹה: לְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ?
Spelled with a final ה although it is pronounced efó.
subtleties: “Where are you from?” is מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה? (מֵ = from).

profile.feeling: Here and now, everyday speech.

phrases.meaning: that’s the crux of the matter

synonyms.nuance: the same meaning, a little more formal; typical of signs, news and writing
“(to) here” with verbs of motion: בּוֹא הֵנָּה! “come here!”

etymology.text: Compare with Egyptian pj (“this”).

funFacts: The idiom פֹּה קָבוּר הַכֶּלֶב is a calque of German “Da liegt der Hund begraben”.
pitfalls: Homograph: פֶּה “mouth” is also written פה without vowels.
“Come here” uses הֵנָּה (direction): בּוֹא הֵנָּה, not פֹּה.
subtleties: פֹּה is the everyday word; כָּאן is equally correct but sounds a little more formal.

profile.feeling: Signs, announcements, a slightly more careful “here”.

examples.tr: Is the station far from here?

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word, a little more casual

etymology.text: From כְּ־ + אָן (“where”).

funFacts: Israel’s public broadcaster (since 2017) is called כָּאן — “here”.
The old word אָן “whither” lives on in לְאָן “where to?”.
pitfalls: כָּאן (kan, here) vs כֵּן (ken, yes): only the vowel differs.
subtleties: עַד כָּאן! can mean “that’s enough!” — and closes a news item.

lexemes.role: question particle: opens a yes/no question (formal and written; in speech rising intonation alone is enough)
marks a definite direct object (no English equivalent): אֲנִי אוֹכֵל אֶת הַגֶּזֶר
to, for; with יֵשׁ / אֵין it marks the possessor (יֵשׁ לִי “I have”). With a pronoun it takes suffixes and is written as a word of its own.

absent.reason: No separate word: the definite article ha- (הַ, also הָ / הֶ before gutturals) is a prefix and is stored in the DEF cells of every noun.
Hebrew has no indefinite article: a bare noun is indefinite (גֶּזֶר = a carrot / carrots). אֶחָד / אַחַת (“one”) can be added for emphasis.
